THE wealth of material brought to lit^lU by the excavations conducted by M. Ernest de Sarzec at Telloh in Babylonia, since 1878, is a boon to ever>- student of the ancient East.

The artistic grace, the diverse methods of writing, and the great varict\-, of these 'finds' m.ike them of first importance in any study of the most ancient periods of the history of lower Bab}-lonia. The unstinted liberality of the French Government in promoting these excavations at Telloh, and its praiseworth_\- care in preserving and exhibiting in the Louvre the results of these treasure-finds, cannot be too highly commended. A goodly number of the inscriptions contained in the Telloh exhibits have been jniblished in the handsome work edited b}- Ernest de Sarzec and Leon Heuzey since 1884.'-'
These splendid reproductions, b}' an almost inimitable French art, have almost precluded the necessity of consulting the original statues, tablets, and stela;.
A The great Cylinders and B are the most notable inscriptions in this publication.
A Double plates 33 and 34, issued in 1S84, present Cylinder executed by a heliograph
A process. In 1887, this same Cylinder was issued again on double plate 35, presenting six views, covering the cylinder, as the result of a direct photographic process. In 1889, Cylinder

B was issued on double plate 36 in six views by the same process. These beautiful reproductions on double plates 35 and 36 are, however, reductions of the originals by more than one-half These reductions, together with an occasional abrasion, and several portions almost hidden b\' calcareous deposits, present practical difficulties in deciphering all of the signs of either of the c\dinders. The only other attempt to present the inscriptions of these cylinders, was in the publication, in the Revue d^\ss\Tiologie,*-- of Amiaud's copy of Cylinder B from among his posthumous manuscripts. This copy, in so far as Amiaud was able to make identifications, is a transliteration into the late Assyrian character, while unidentified signs are a transcript of the original. Several long omissions in this copy, due doubtless to the fact that it was made for private use only, rendered it quite desirable that as complete a transcript as possible of these great cylinders be made accessible to scholars. Therefore, at the suggestion of Professor Friedrich Delitzsch, the author went to
Paris, in the spring of 1898, to undertake the work. By the kindness of M. Leon Heuzey, Coiiservateiir dcs Antiquitcs orieiitalcs in the
Louvre, ready access was granted to the valuable documents of the Telloh collection, and
A permission given to copy the great CyHnders and B of Gudea.

A The difficulties of the work at the beginning were twofold: (i) lack of large experience in copying inscriptions directly from clay originals, and (2) the fact that the reading had to be done through the plate-glass of the case that contained the cylinders (see the
Diconvertes c-n Chahlie. Par Ernest de Sarzec, |iublie [lar les soins de Leon Heuzey. — Vols. II. pp. 124—135; III. pp. 42 4S.

A picture, on p. VI. taken b}- the author while in the midst of his work. Cylinder on the left, and Cylinder B occupies the right end of the case). The first difficult}', during more than forty days, or 200 hours, of close work, gradually wore awa\-. But the second was a continual menace to the eyes, especially when obliged to use a magnifying glass, requiring at the same time an especial effort to overcome the glare caused by the two surfaces of glass.

A Cylinder is a hollow clay cylinder. 61 centimeters in length and ^2 cent, in diameter, the rim of clay being about two cent, thick. Although this cylinder had been broken into pieces, these pieces have been gathered up and nicely adjusted, with the loss of but a few fragments. The surface is quite well preserved, aside from a few places unfortunately rubbed, and others covered with a semi-transparent hard deposit. These places were read, where read at all, only with difficulty.' Some assistance was secured by the use of a mirror, casting upon the doubtful portion a strong ray of sunlight, and then magnifying

A such special place. Cylinder carries thirty columns, averaging about eighty lines (not cases) to the column. The first-half of the inscription is more compactly and solidly written than the latter part; the scribe apparently discovered that he was not obliged to crowd his matter to find room for all of it on the cylinder, and thereafter wrote more loosely.

B Cylinder is also a hollow cla\- cylinder, 56 cent, in length, and 33 cent, in diameter, the rim of clay being about two cent, thick. It contained originally twenty-four columns, averaging about sixty lines to the column. With a less number of columns and a le.ss number of lines to the column, and a slightly larger diameter than Cylinder A, the signcharacters are larger and the whole inscription is more loosely written than Cylinder A. This cylinder also had been broken into pieces, but has been carefully readjusted. Unfortunately nearly all of the last quarter of it is lost, together with small pieces here and there
A in the body of the inscription.
few portions, too, have been damaged by a hard deposit, but the size of the signs is more of an aid to the decipherer than those on Cylinder A.

A Cylinders and B together, in their present form, carry more than 10,600 charac— — ters, and, as will be seen by the Sign-List (pp. 89 11 1), more than 325 different signs, many of them peculiar to these c_\-linders.

In the revision of his first readings the author had the valuable assistance of the e.xpert Assyriologist and attache of the Louvre, M. Frangois Thureau-Dangin. His skilled eye rendered especial aid in the reading of the earlier parts of cols. X, XI, and XII of C}'linder
A, and in the damaged and partially deposit-covered portions of cols. IV and \'II of
Cylinder B, as well as in the depiction here and there of individual signs.

In the autographic work, the author has endeavored to transmit to paper as nearly as possible, both the size of the column and the form of the sign, contained on the ori— ginal clay, even to some apparent mistakes of the scribe, for example, in Cylinder A, IV, 9, /(?;-, in 12, ;/, etc. The variations in the number of wedges in many signs reveal the fact that considerable liberty was allowed in the formation of the characters (see Sign-List
A for variations). The author's reproduction of na in Cylinder should have, at the right end of the horizontal line, as it has in Cylinder B, but one instead tivo wedge-heads.

The author, too, has labored under the disadvantage of being absent from the originals in his autographic work. This may result, on further investigation, in discovering some erroneous readings. But he ventures to hope that these may be so few as not to invalidate the great body of the inscriptions.

Several questions of vital importance in cuneiform research have been suggested in connection with the stnd\- of these and other (nulean inscriptions: (I) The direction of writing and of reading these earl)' inscriptions, is a question that finds no adequate solution in the writings of these cylinders. May it not have been that these cylinders were supported on some kind of a horizontal axis and turned on this axis before the eyes of the reader, to be read in the same position as were the inscriptions on the statues of Gudea, from above — downwards and proceeiling from right to left.^ (2) The origin of the cuneiform writing receives for its solution slight aid from these cylinders, because of a probable wide departure from the original forms in the adoption and liberal use of the wedge-head. The hte'rature on the Gudean inscriptions will receive attention in the Introtluclion to Part II, which the author hopes to have in press in the autumn.
